headlines.article_text: CVS to split off drugstore business Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half of 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate splits in history. The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs. In this article CVS Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A person walks into a CVS pharmacy near George Washington University in Washington, U.S., August 15, 2024. Kaylee Greenlee Beal | Reuters CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate splits in history, the company announced Wednesday. The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would specifically separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs. The decision follows a "comprehensive strategic review" by the company's board of directors, according to a news release. It's a stunning reversal for the healthcare powerhouse, which has spent the last two decades working to turn itself into a one-stop health destination. The move also comes as CVS' aggressive turnaround plan under CEO David Joyner shows substantial progress, with the company pursuing $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shakeups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs. "From a position of strength, and a focus on the long term, we plan to create two focused companies to improve consumer engagement, affordability, and care coordination," Joyner said in the release. CVS shares have jumped roughly 70% since Joyner took the helm in October 2024, bringing the company's market value to $117 billion. The two new companies would both be publicly traded. The insurance and PBM company will retain the CVS Health name and be run by Joyner, while the other company will be called CVS Pharmacy and be led by Prem Shah, who is currently group president of CVS Health. Additional leadership positions and board members will be announced at a later date, CVS said. Existing CVS shareholders will own shares in both companies after the split. The Financial Times on Tuesday first reported the breakup plans. The company's pharmacy business raked in $37.66 billion in 2025 sales, while its insurance unit booked $36.29 billion in revenue and healthcare services segment generated $51.24 billion. CVS on Wednesday also posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that topped Wall Street expectations. Total sales climbed to $108.40 billion, from $102.87 billion in the prior-year period. Sales were boosted by year-over-year growth in the company's health care benefits and health services segments. Meanwhile, revenue in its pharmacy services business slid from the previous year. How the CVS split would work On Wednesday, CVS said it will lump its insurer and PBM with its primary care business Oak Street Health, home-visit provider Signify Health and the company's specialty drug business. CVS also said the split will allow the two companies to experience a "focused strategic agenda" and greater ability to "innovate, adopt technology, increase efficiency," among other benefits. It's not the first time CVS has weighed splitting the company. In October 2024, CVS engaged advisors in a strategic review of its business and considered breaking up its retail pharmacy and insurance units. Even so, Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny said the split "feels like a complete shock" in a Tuesday note. But he said that the retail pharmacy business has been performing well, winning market share from competitors and seeing stabilizing gross margins thanks to CostVantage, a new pharmacy reimbursement model introduced by CVS last year. "In this context, perhaps the outlook for a standalone retail pharmacy (still with meaningful scale and leverage on its own) is stronger now than before," Cherny wrote. He added that "the rationale could also be to avoid what has been relentless state legislative scrutiny over the company's level of vertical integration." The potential breakup also comes as pharmacy benefit managers face mounting bipartisan scrutiny in Washington, D.C., and across states. PBMs, which negotiate drug prices and manage prescription drug benefits on behalf of insurers and employers, have been criticized for opaque pricing practices, their growing market power and potential conflicts of interest when they are owned by companies that also operate insurers and pharmacies. Congress enacted PBM reforms in February, including provisions to change how PBMs are compensated under Medicare Part D. Meanwhile, states have increasingly moved to restrict PBMs' ownership of pharmacies. Qualcomm said the deal represents its largest 5G initiative to date. SpaceX, which currently beams Starlink broadband internet to millions of subscribers in the U.S. via satellites in low-earth orbit, is turning to Qualcomm for terrestrial expansion. In this article SPCX QCOM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 0:53 00:53 SpaceX signs deal with Qualcomm to provide network technology for U.S. mobile service Squawk Box SpaceX announced a deal with chipmaker Qualcomm to provide key network technology for Elon Musk's Starlink Mobile service, a challenger to Verizon , AT&T and T-Mobile . Qualcomm said on Wednesday that the terrestrial network it will help SpaceX build will "complement Starlink's satellite capabilities," with a planned rollout to begin next year. Financial terms of the multiyear deal weren't disclosed. "Together with SpaceX, we are building world-leading cellular infrastructure in the United States, advancing 5G today, with an opportunity to lay the foundation for AI-native 6G in the years ahead," Durga Malladi, an executive vice president at Qualcomm, said in the statement. Starlink is a critical piece of SpaceX's business, accounting for 36% of the company's revenue in the third quarter and 85% of its operating profit. But to date, the company's consumer business has been limited when it comes to mobile direct-to-device services as its satellite network can't provide all the voice, video and data coverage that competitors offer on popular smartphones. Now SpaceX is snapping up spectrum and forging partnerships to take on the major mobile carriers. Last month, the company announced an agreement to purchase a nationwide spectrum portfolio in the 800 MHz band. The news sent shares of U.S. carriers reeling. Earlier this week, the Washington Post reported that SpaceX is in talks to acquire EchoStar's Boost Mobile. SpaceX went public in June in the largest IPO on record and is now valued at close to $2 trillion. watch now VIDEO 4:35 04:35 Faber Report: SpaceX buys spectrum to expand Starlink mobile service Squawk on the Street With Qualcomm, SpaceX will be using the chipmaker's Dragonwing cellular infrastructure hardware and software in base stations to enable high-capacity coverage for Starlink Mobile. Qualcomm has a long history of making chips for cellular networks, but is best known for making the modems and radios that go inside devices, not base stations for running a wireless network. The company has targeted carriers and other infrastructure companies since it made a bigger push into the 5G infrastructure market in 2020 . SpaceX represents one of Qualcomm's highest-profile customers or partners in 5G infrastructure, following earlier deals with Verizon, Dish, and Europe's Vodafone. While SpaceX plans to use Qualcomm's technology to establish tens of thousands of new cell sites, it hasn't announced partners among cell tower companies or said how many new towers may be required. Mobile carriers generally lease space from companies such as American Tower and Crown Castle , which commonly host multiple carriers from one site. SpaceX did not respond to CNBC's request for additional information. -- CNBC's Kif Leswing contributed reporting. headlines.title: Stocks making the biggest moves premarket: Trump Media, Tesla, CoreWeave, Novo Nordisk and more
headlines.summary: These are the stocks posting the largest moves in the premarket.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves premarket: DJT, TSLA, CRWV, NVO Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Check out the companies making the biggest moves in premarket trading: Trump Media & Technology Group — Shares of President Donald Trump 's social media company and tech company were down 11% after a decisive victory by Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections Tuesday night. Trump owns 41% of the company, which owns social media platform Truth Social. Democrats taking control of Congress add a check on the president's policies. Tesla , SpaceX — Shares of Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX dropped nearly 6% and more than 7%, respectively. The moves come after the Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate. Many of the newly elected candidates have critical positions on the rapid data center build-out that's been fueled by artificial intelligence. SpaceX operates an AI supercomputing infrastructure in Tennessee and Mississippi , while Tesla has one in Texas. Neocloud stocks — Shares of so-called neocloud companies moved lower, with CoreWeave dropping 7%, Iren tumbling 6% and Nebius slipping about 5%. The Democratic wins in Texas and rejection of data centers in ballots across the country is expected to create hurdles for data center plays. Novo Nordisk — Shares gained over 6% after the global healthcare company reported earnings of 5.79 Danish kroner, or about 63 cents per share, compared with Wall Street expectations of 5.10 kroner, or about 55 cents. The company raised its fiscal 2026 outlook, citing expectations for GLP-1 product sales. CVS Health — Shares fell more than 2% after the company said it would split into two separate publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028. The move would reverse CVS' $78 billion acquisition of Aetna and separate the company's retail pharmacy business. McDonald's — The fast-food restaurant chain reported mixed quarterly results , sending shares 2% higher. Adjusted earnings came in at $3.57 per share, topping the $3.38 expected from analysts polled by LSEG. However, its revenue of $7.16 billion fell short of the $7.29 billion consensus estimate. Duolingo — The language learning software company surged 18% after reporting third-quarter revenue of $309 million. That topped an LSEG consensus of $303 million. Monthly active users totaled 153 million for the quarter, exceeding a 149 million forecast. Adjusted EBITDA margin also topped expectations. Alight — The employee benefits consultancy popped 22% after raising its outlook for the full-year 2026. Alight sees revenue in a range of $2.115 billion to $2.125 billion, versus the FactSet consensus estimate of $2.09 billion. Adjusted EBITDA guidance of $410 million to $420 million also beat the Street's estimates of $404.4 million. Avis Budget Group — The car rental agency slid about 2% on mixed third-quarter results. Avis earned $5.15 a share, a steep decline from $10.11 per share in the year-earlier period. Revenue clocked in at $3.44 billion, slightly ahead of a FactSet consensus of $3.42 billion. Advanced Micro Devices — The chipmaker was last little changed after reporting stronger-than-expected third-quarter earnings . Adjusted earnings of $2.09 per share topped estimates for $1.95, according to analysts polled by LSEG. Revenue forecasts for the current quarter also came in above estimates. Toast — The restaurant management software company dropped 5% despite delivering third-quarter results that topped estimates, according to FactSet. Toast also said CFO Elena Gomez will leave the company at the end of 2026 and will be replaced by senior vice president of finance Michael Senno. Skyworks Solutions — The provider of wireless networking services slumped about 11% after guidance for the current quarter disappointed the Street. Skyworks anticipates adjusted earnings of about $1.25 per share and revenue of $1.80 billion to $1.90 billion in the fiscal first quarter, short of LSEG consensus estimates of $1.50 a share and $1.99 billion. Skyworks completed its combination with Qorvo in early October, and the first quarter marks the first combined quarter for the two. Super Micro Computer — Shares of the server company jumped 2% after Super Micro earnings per share and revenue beat Wall Street estimates. For fiscal year 2027, the company expects net sales to range between $72 billion and $82 billion, above the LSEG consensus for $69.17 billion. Arista Networks — The cloud networking company gained 4% after current-quarter guidance topped estimates. Arista sees fourth-quarter earnings of $1.26 to $1.30 per share on revenue of $3.9 billion to $4.0 billion. Analysts surveyed by LSEG were looking for $1.15 per share and $3.60 billion. Block — The fintech stock rallied 9% after Block posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that exceeded expectations, and raised guidance for the full year ending December. Adjusted earnings of $1.13 per share topped the $1.03 LSEG consensus estimate, while revenue of $6.72 billion beat the $6.59 billion consensus. Freshworks — The software stock tumbled about 10% even after the customer support ticketing company posted stronger-than-expected third-quarter results and full-year guidance. Freshworks earned an adjusted 22 cents per share on revenue of $245.4 million in the latest quarter, above earnings of 18 cents on revenue of $245.1 million analysts polled by FactSet expected. The stock has recently outperformed, rallying more than 20% over the past three months. Renewable energy stocks — Shares of renewable energy companies moved higher after the Democratic sweep of Congress. Sunrun , Nextpower and Plug Power each climbed roughly 6%, while Canadian Solar moved 7% higher and First Solar jumped nearly 8%. Amdocs — The software stock tumbled 37% after the company's warning that its revenue could fall as much as 18% in fiscal 2027 as a result of its dispute with T-Mobile over existing agreements, a completion of an integration project with U.S. Cellular customers and a reduction in T-Mobile's discretionary spending. Datadog — The cloud monitoring company sank 17% after releasing its third-quarter financial results. While it beat on both the top and bottom lines, its revenue guidance came in soft. Datadog expects revenue of $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion for the fourth quarter, versus the $1.20 billion consensus estimate. Shares had already run 62% higher this year. Kraft Heinz — The food and beverage manufacturer gained 3%. Kraft Heinz said it will dives t its North America coffee business to One Rock Capital Partners. The company also reported adjusted earnings of 53 cents per share on revenue of $6.12 billion for its third quarter, topping expectations. Analysts polled by LSEG had expected EPS of 42 cents on revenue of $6.09 billion. — CNBC's Darla Mercado, Deena Zaidi, Paulina Likos, Sarah Min, Davis Giangiulio, Ananya Chetia and Fred Imbert contributed reporting.

In this article MCD Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT McDonald's logo sign is seen in Berlin, Germany, on September 12, 2026. Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty Images McDonald's on Wednesday reported mixed quarterly results as traffic to its U.S. restaurants fell, leading to a slight decline in domestic same-store sales. The fast-food giant reported a 0.2% decrease in sales at its U.S. restaurants that have been open at least 13 months. Even so, the segment performed better than the 0.5% decline that Wall Street anticipated, according to a survey of analysts by StreetAccount. At the company's investor day in September, executives said that same-store sales in July and August were slightly negative but they expected September to return to same-store sales growth. "In the U.S., we're encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value," McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski said in a statement. Kempczinski said in August that the company's U.S. business was falling short on execution, particularly on the implementation of its value offerings. Like many restaurants, McDonald's has leaned into discounts to attract budget-conscious diners over the last two years. Shares of the company rose more than 2% in premarket trading. Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $3.57 adjusted vs. $3.38 expected Revenue: $7.16 billion vs. $7.29 billion expected The company reported third-quarter net income of $2.49 billion, or $3.51 per share, up from $2.28 billion, or $3.18 per share, a year earlier. Excluding restructuring charges and other items, McDonald's earned $3.57 per share. Net revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion. The company's same-store sales rose 1.5%, lifted by its international segments. That topped analysts' expectations of a 1.3% increase, according to StreetAccount. McDonald's international developmental licensed markets business, which includes Japan and China, reported same-store sales growth of 4.2%. Wall Street was forecasting same-store sales to rise 2.1% for the division, based on StreetAccount estimates. The company's international operated division, which includes top markets like Australia and Germany, saw same-store sales growth of 1.4%. Still, the business underperformed Wall Street's expectations. Analysts were projecting same-store sales would rise 2.1%, according to StreetAccount. France was a weak spot, McDonald's said. headlines.summary: AI fortunes were mixed as premarket trading opened on Wednesday.
headlines.article_text: SpaceX, Tesla stocks fall over 4% on Democrats big win Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Several AI-linked stocks fell as election results came in showing a convincing win by Democrats of both houses of Congress. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor’s race after campaigning for tougher limits on data center development. Investors are weighing whether state-level data center restrictions could delay projects in major buildout markets. In this article CRWV TSLA SPCX NBIS NVDA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT State Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the 2026 Democratic nominee for Texas governor, speaks at an Arlington, Texas, campaign rally on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. She faces Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, in the Nov. 3 general election. (Eleanor Dearman/Fort Worth Star-Telegram/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) Eleanor Dearman | Fort Worth Star-Telegram | Getty Images AI data center stocks came under pressure as Democrats — seen as proponents of moratoriums on the buildout — won big in midterm elections and in key technology hubs like Texas. Markets were already anticipating the Democrats to win the House of Representatives and possibly take Senate control. But the Texas governor mansion going to Democrats was a big blow, analysts said. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who wants to enact an immediate moratorium on data centers in the state, won over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. According to Wells Fargo, 27% of planned data center gigawatts is in the Lone Star State. The midterm elections will slow the pace of data center buildouts across the U.S., Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note on Wednesday morning. "There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," he said. He added that the election in Texas was the "biggest worry" of the night for tech investors and the AI trade because that's where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from. Shares of Elon Musk 's SpaceX shed 7%. The Democrats' victory in Texas is a big setback for Musk , where he heavily backed Republican candidates, and where his companies Tesla and SpaceX are based. Musk spent a record of at least $474 million on the midterms and funneled $224 million into Texas alone, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott lost to Democrats. SpaceX is currently building out multiple gigawatts of data center capacity, including projects in Texas. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said in a post on X in the early hours on Wednesday, referring to his speculative plans to build AI infrastructure off-planet. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Iren fell by 7% and 6%, respectively. Peer Nebius Group was down 3% and Oracle shed 4.3%. Nvidia shares were slightly in the red. Tech giants Alphabet , Meta and Microsoft mostly bucked the trend and were higher. The Democratic win in Texas adds to existing pressure on the bull-market-leading AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 index fell into correction territory to end October as concerns mounted that the growth of data center spending by big hyperscalers and private AI juggernauts OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing. "We believe the equity market reaction from the midterms mostly depends on the outcome of the Texas governor's race — a Dem win could potentially be a left-tail event to the AI trade, warned Ohsung Kwon, Wells Fargo's chief equity strategist, in a report this week. Democrats won or retained the governorships in other key data center states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio. Georgia represents 7% of all the planned U.S. datacenter gigawatts, while Ohio and Pennsylvania account for 5% apiece, estimates Wells Fargo. Notable investment strategist Michael Hartnett of Bank of America warned earlier this year that Democrats winning the Senate, combined with taking the Texas governorship could lead to a "big slump" in stocks of more than 10% into year-end.
